title: GAN training is delicate and unstable
description: The authors state that training standard GANs is well known for being delicate and unstable.
canonical_description: standard GAN training is delicate and unstable

verdict.reasoning: The subsequent literature directly confronts the claimed delicacy/instability of GAN training. MSG-GAN is the strongest driver: it explicitly frames training instability as its target problem and demonstrates stable convergence across datasets, resolutions, loss functions, and architectures with fixed hyperparameters, including a quantitative stability metric showing stable convergence where ProGAN does not. WGAN-GP reinforces this by diagnosing a concrete failure mechanism (weight clipping in the Wasserstein critic) and replacing it with a gradient-penalty scheme shown to stabilize a wide class of GANs, including without batch normalization. These together directly address the canonical claim for the dominant image-synthesis setting. Confidence is moderated rather than high because the gap is stated maximally broadly and the solution is not total: MSG-GAN's evidence is confined to image synthesis (not non-image modalities or very large-scale conditional settings), WGAN-GP still introduces tunable hyperparameters (lambda, n_critic), and the auxiliary methods (AEGAN, CDE-GAN) each stabilize only under narrow or heavily modified training regimes. So the core "training is unstable" problem is substantially answered, but residual sensitivity and generality limits remain.

paper.title: Improved Training of Wasserstein GANs
paper.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are powerful generative models, but suffer from training instability. The recently proposed Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) makes progress toward stable training of GANs, but sometimes can still generate only low-quality samples or fail to converge. We find that these problems are often due to the use of weight clipping in WGAN to enforce a Lipschitz constraint on the critic, which can lead to undesired behavior. We propose an alternative to clipping weights: penalize the norm of gradient of the critic with respect to its input. Our proposed method performs better than standard WGAN and enables stable training of a wide variety of GAN architectures with almost no hyperparameter tuning, including 101-layer ResNets and language models over discrete data. We also achieve high quality generations on CIFAR-10 and LSUN bedrooms.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper diagnoses a major source of GAN/WGAN training instability — weight clipping used to enforce the Lipschitz constraint on the critic — and proposes an alternative that penalizes the norm of the critic's gradient w.r.t. its input (WGAN-GP). It proves that the optimal critic under this scheme has unit gradient norm almost everywhere, and empirically shows the proposed procedure converges stably across many architectures (e.g., without batch normalization) and datasets, outperforming standard WGAN and other GAN training procedures. This directly targets the claimed delicacy/instability of GAN training.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper addresses instability specifically for the Wasserstein-GAN family (critic-based optimization with a Lipschitz constraint enforced by a gradient penalty). It does not fully solve the broad problem of standard GAN training being delicate and unstable across all settings: instability and mode collapse can still occur in other GAN variants and conditions, and the method itself introduces new hyperparameters (penalty coefficient lambda, n_critic) whose tuning is still delicate. Thus it stabilizes a large class of GAN training but does not eliminate the overall instability/delicacy problem.
evidence_snippets: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are powerful generative models, but suffer from training instability. The recently proposed Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) makes progress toward stable training of GANs, but sometimes can still generate only low-quality samples or fail to converge.

We find that these problems are often due to the use of weight clipping in WGAN to enforce a Lipschitz constraint on the critic, which can lead to undesired behavior. We propose an alternative to clipping weights: penalize the norm of gradient of the critic with respect to its input.

We show that our proposed method performs better than standard WGAN and also better than other common GAN training procedures, under a variety of architectures and with or without batch normalization.

paper.title: MSG-GAN: Multi-Scale Gradients for Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: While Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have seen huge successes in image synthesis tasks, they are notoriously difficult to adapt to different datasets, in part due to instability during training and sensitivity to hyperparameters. One commonly accepted reason for this instability is that gradients passing from the discriminator to the generator become uninformative when there isn't enough overlap in the supports of the real and fake distributions. In this work, we propose the Multi-Scale Gradient Generative Adversarial Network (MSG-GAN), a simple but effective technique for addressing this by allowing the flow of gradients from the discriminator to the generator at multiple scales. This technique provides a stable approach for high resolution image synthesis, and serves as an alternative to the commonly used progressive growing technique. We show that MSG-GAN converges stably on a variety of image datasets of different sizes, resolutions and domains, as well as different types of loss functions and architectures, all with the same set of fixed hyperparameters. When compared to state-of-the-art GANs, our approach matches or exceeds the performance in most of the cases we tried.

assessments.contribution_summary: MSG-GAN directly targets the stated gap: it identifies GAN training instability (caused by uninformative gradients when real/fake supports don't overlap) as its core problem and proposes a concrete architectural remedy — feeding the discriminator generator outputs at multiple scales so gradients flow from the discriminator to the generator at all resolutions simultaneously. It validates this with extensive stability evidence: fixed hyperparameters across datasets of different sizes/resolutions/domains, robustness across loss functions and base architectures, convergence on multiple learning rates, and a quantitative stability measure (MSE between samples from fixed latents across epochs) showing MSG-ProGAN converges stably while ProGAN does not.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper solves the instability problem substantially but only for the image-synthesis setting it evaluates, and it does not close the gap in full generality: it does not address training instability for non-image modalities, class-conditional/large-scale settings such as BigGAN, or completely eliminate sensitivity (the authors note MSG-StyleGAN could not beat StyleGAN's FID on CelebA-HQ/FFHQ, and the method cannot use StyleGAN's mixing regularization). The paper also leaves combinations with orthogonal stabilizers (e.g., VDB) to future work and frames some robustness differences (realism vs. diversity trade-off) as open questions. Within its demonstrated scope (multi-scale image generation on the tested datasets, losses, and architectures) the instability problem is directly and substantially addressed.
evidence_snippets: While Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have seen huge successes in image synthesis tasks, they are notoriously difficult to adapt to different datasets, in part due to instability during training and sensitivity to hyperparameters.
In this work, however, we address the problem of training instability.

We show that MSG-GAN converges stably on a variety of image datasets of different sizes, resolutions and domains, as well as different types of loss functions and architectures, all with the same set of \emph{fixed} hyperparameters.

paper.title: Autoencoding Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: In the years since Goodfellow et al. introduced Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), there has been an explosion in the breadth and quality of generative model applications. Despite this work, GANs still have a long way to go before they see mainstream adoption, owing largely to their infamous training instability. Here I propose the Autoencoding Generative Adversarial Network (AEGAN), a four-network model which learns a bijective mapping between a specified latent space and a given sample space by applying an adversarial loss and a reconstruction loss to both the generated images and the generated latent vectors. The AEGAN technique offers several improvements to typical GAN training, including training stabilization, mode-collapse prevention, and permitting the direct interpolation between real samples. The effectiveness of the technique is illustrated using an anime face dataset.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes AEGAN, a four-network autoencoding GAN (generator + encoder + two discriminators) that augments the standard adversarial objective with reconstruction losses in both directions (images reconstructed through G(E(x)) and latent vectors through E(G(z))). The stated purpose is precisely to stabilize GAN training and prevent mode collapse by giving the generator direct access to the data manifold and forcing a bijective latent<->sample mapping. Empirically, on a 64x64 anime-face dataset, AEGAN is compared against a standard GAN and an AAE with identical architectures; across repeated random-initialization runs the GAN undergoes total mode collapse while AEGAN does not, and AEGAN produces sharper reconstructions than the AAE.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap is broad and general ("standard GAN training is delicate and unstable"), whereas the paper supplies only one specific architectural remedy validated under limited conditions. It does not establish that AEGAN stabilizes GAN training generally: the experiments use a single small anime-face dataset, a deliberately simplistic implementation (no batch normalization, Wasserstein loss, progressive growing, or conditioning), and no comparison against established stabilizers. Residual instability/artifacts remain even in-domain (oscillatory cycling through eye colors during training, uniformly green eyes, degraded male faces and glasses), and no theoretical account of stability is given. Whether the method transfers to other domains, higher resolutions, or combination with modern GAN techniques is left as future work, so the general problem of delicate/unstable standard GAN training is only partially addressed.
evidence_snippets: The AEGAN technique stabilizes GAN training by directing the generator towards the low-dimensional manifold in high-dimensional pixel space.

To verify that the stark differences in results were not a fluke, the AEGAN and the GAN were both trained from random initialization for 300k training steps five additional times; in each case, the GAN underwent total mode collapse while the AEGAN did not.
The primary limitation of this particular experiment is that the GAN implementation ... is fairly simplistic due to time and resource constraints.

paper.title: CDE-GAN: Cooperative Dual Evolution Based Generative Adversarial Network
paper.abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have been a popular deep generative model for real-world applications. Despite many recent efforts on GANs that have been contributed, mode collapse and instability of GANs are still open problems caused by their adversarial optimization difficulties. In this paper, motivated by the cooperative co-evolutionary algorithm, we propose a Cooperative Dual Evolution based Generative Adversarial Network (CDE-GAN) to circumvent these drawbacks. In essence, CDE-GAN incorporates dual evolution with respect to the generator(s) and discriminators into a unified evolutionary adversarial framework to conduct effective adversarial multi-objective optimization. Thus it exploits the complementary properties and injects dual mutation diversity into training to steadily diversify the estimated density in capturing multi-modes and improve generative performance. Specifically, CDE-GAN decomposes the complex adversarial optimization problem into two subproblems (generation and discrimination), and each subproblem is solved with a separated subpopulation (E-Generator} and E-Discriminators), evolved by its own evolutionary algorithm. Additionally, we further propose a Soft Mechanism to balance the trade-off between E-Generators and E-Discriminators to conduct steady training for CDE-GAN. Extensive experiments on one synthetic dataset and three real-world benchmark image datasets demonstrate that the proposed CDE-GAN achieves a competitive and superior performance in generating good quality and diverse samples over baselines. The code and more generated results are available at our project homepage: https://shiming-chen.github.io/CDE-GAN-website/CDE-GAN.html.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly targets the instability (and mode collapse) of GAN training, the exact concern named in the gap. It proposes CDE-GAN, which decomposes the adversarial min-max problem into two subproblems (generation and discrimination) solved by co-evolving subpopulations — E-Generators and E-Discriminators — each undergoing its own mutations, fitness evaluation, and selection, bridged by a "Soft Mechanism" that weakens discriminators to keep training balanced. Experiments on a synthetic 8-Gaussian dataset and CIFAR-10, LSUN-Bedrooms, and CelebA report higher inception scores and steadier training curves than baselines (e.g., E-GAN, WGAN, LSGAN, MAD-GAN, Lipizzaner), with the paper attributing stability to informative gradients from multiple discriminators and dual mutation diversity.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not resolve the general claim that standard GAN training is delicate and unstable: instead of stabilizing the standard formulation, it replaces it with a substantially modified, heavier training paradigm (dual evolutionary populations, multiple mutations, Soft Mechanism with δ, fitness trade-off γ, population sizes I/J, etc.), and its evidence is purely empirical on a limited set of datasets/architectures with no convergence or stability guarantees. It also only mitigates, not eliminates, instability, and the paper itself notes the cost of roughly O(K·I·N)+O(J·M) per generator iteration. A principled, general, and cheap way to make vanilla/minimax GAN training robust remains open.
evidence_snippets: mode collapse and instability of GANs are still open problems caused by their adversarial optimization difficulties. In this paper, motivated by the cooperative co-evolutionary algorithm, we propose a \textit{Cooperative Dual Evolution based Generative Adversarial Network} (CDE-GAN) to circumvent these drawbacks.

CDE-GAN terms adversarial training as an adversarial multi-objective optimization problem, and thus the multiple discriminators provide informative feedback gradient to the generator for stabilizing training process.

paper.title: Gang of GANs: Generative Adversarial Networks with Maximum Margin Ranking
paper.abstract: Traditional generative adversarial networks (GAN) and many of its variants are trained by minimizing the KL or JS-divergence loss that measures how close the generated data distribution is from the true data distribution. A recent advance called the WGAN based on Wasserstein distance can improve on the KL and JS-divergence based GANs, and alleviate the gradient vanishing, instability, and mode collapse issues that are common in the GAN training. In this work, we aim at improving on the WGAN by first generalizing its discriminator loss to a margin-based one, which leads to a better discriminator, and in turn a better generator, and then carrying out a progressive training paradigm involving multiple GANs to contribute to the maximum margin ranking loss so that the GAN at later stages will improve upon early stages. We call this method Gang of GANs (GoGAN). We have shown theoretically that the proposed GoGAN can reduce the gap between the true data distribution and the generated data distribution by at least half in an optimally trained WGAN. We have also proposed a new way of measuring GAN quality which is based on image completion tasks. We have evaluated our method on four visual datasets: CelebA, LSUN Bedroom, CIFAR-10, and 50K-SSFF, and have seen both visual and quantitative improvement over baseline WGAN.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes GoGAN, which builds on the Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) by (1) generalizing WGAN's discriminator loss to a margin-based (hinge) loss, called MGAN, and (2) adding a progressive, multi-stage training paradigm with a maximum-margin ranking loss that ties adjacent-stage discriminators/generators together. The claimed benefits are a stronger discriminator leading to a stronger generator, a theoretical guarantee that the distribution gap is reduced by at least half (at WGAN-optimal equilibrium), a new image-completion-based quality metric, and empirical PSNR/SSIM improvements over WGAN on CelebA, LSUN Bedroom, CIFAR-10, and 50K-SSFF. The paper takes WGAN's stability advantages as given prior art and focuses on improving generation quality, not on making training itself stable or robust.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not tackle the gap's specific problem — the delicacy/instability of (standard) GAN training. It never analyzes gradient behavior, convergence robustness, mode collapse, oscillation, or sensitivity of training to hyperparameters, nor does it claim or demonstrate that its margin/ranking scheme makes training more stable. Instead it presupposes WGAN's stability (stated as already solving "the gradient vanishing, instability, and mode collapse issues") and proposes improvements aimed at output quality and distribution-gap reduction. Its theoretical result holds only under strong assumptions (an optimally trained WGAN at equilibrium), and the added multi-stage ranking machinery could plausibly add training complexity rather than remove it — but no stability analysis or evidence on this is provided. What remains open is any method, analysis, or empirical demonstration that directly stabilizes or makes less delicate the adversarial training of GANs.
